sections.label: Choice of Court Agreements Bill
sections.summary: The Bill gives effect to the 2005 Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements, which upholds exclusive choice of court agreements and governs judgment recognition and enforcement.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: The Choice of Court Agreements Bill seeks to give effect to the Convention on Choice of Court Agreements done at The Hague on 30 June 2005, which establishes an international legal regime for upholding exclusive choice of court agreements in international civil or commercial cases and governs the recognition and enforcement of judgments amongst parties to the Convention.

sections.label: SIAC record year 2015
sections.summary: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre had a record year in 2015 with 271 new cases involving $6.23 billion in disputes.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) had a record year in 2015, with 271 new cases involving $6.23 billion in disputes.

sections.label: Bill boosts dispute resolution hub
sections.summary: The Bill implements the Convention regime and will boost Singapore's position as a dispute resolution hub in Asia by enhancing international enforceability of Singapore Court judgments.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: The Convention regime, which today's Bill seeks to implement, is one such framework.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: This Bill will boost Singapore's position as a dispute resolution hub in Asia by enhancing the international enforceability of Singapore Court judgments.

sections.label: Singapore signs Convention 2015
sections.summary: Singapore signed the Convention on 25 March 2015, it came into force on 1 October 2015, and there are presently 28 states party to it.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: Singapore signed the Convention on 25 March 2015.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: The Convention came into force on 1 October 2015.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: There are presently 28 states which are parties to the Convention.

sections.label: Enhancing Singapore judgments enforceability
sections.summary: First, it will enhance the enforceability of Singapore judgments in other jurisdictions.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: First, it will enhance the enforceability of Singapore judgments in other jurisdictions.

sections.label: Bill applies to international matters
sections.summary: In line with the Convention, the Bill only applies to international civil or commercial matters.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: In line with the Convention, the Bill only applies to international civil or commercial matters.

sections.label: High Court includes SICC
sections.summary: Clause 2(2) construes references to the High Court in exclusive choice of court agreements as including SICC, unless the agreement shows contrary intention.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: Clause 2(2) of the Bill makes it clear that references to the High Court in an exclusive choice of court agreement to which the Convention applies is to be construed as including SICC, unless a contrary intention appears in the agreement.

sections.label: Recognition of valid foreign judgments
sections.summary: A foreign judgment valid and enforceable in its state of origin will generally be recognised and enforced in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: Generally, where a foreign judgment is valid and enforceable in the state in which the judgment originated, it will be recognised and enforced in Singapore.

sections.label: Singapore signs Hague Convention 2015
sections.summary: Current law would apply in such cases, and Singapore signed the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements on 25 March 2015.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: In such cases, the current law applicable to enforcing such agreements, as well as the recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments, would apply.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: Such implementation and ratification will enhance the overseas enforceability of judgments of our Courts, further incentivise parties to litigate their disputes here, and demonstrate our commitment to contribute towards facilitating international commerce.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: On 25 March 2015, Singapore signed the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements of 2005.

sections.label: Eleven countries plus 28 states
sections.summary: Presently 11 countries' civil judgments may be recognised and enforced in Singapore; the Convention adds 28 states including Mexico and all EU countries except Denmark.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Presently, under our present law, there are only 11 countries whose civil judgments may be recognised and enforceable in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: With the Convention and passing of this Bill, the 11 countries will be joined by another 28 states that include Mexico and all countries in the EU, except Denmark.

sections.label: New York Convention arbitration awards
sections.summary: The New York Convention applies to recognition and enforcement of international arbitration awards and currently has about 156 signatories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The New York Convention applies to the recognition and enforcement of international arbitration awards and currently has about 156 signatories.

sections.label: Courts' decisions and SICC timing
sections.summary: The High Court and Admiralty Courts have landmark international decisions, and the Convention signing and Bill coincide with SICC's setting up in January this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Our High Court and Admiralty Courts have their share of landmark decisions in international jurisprudence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It is not by chance that the signing of this Convention, and now this Bill, coincides with the recent setting up of SICC in January this year.

sections.label: SCMA BIMCO arbitration clause
sections.summary: In 2013 SCMA persuaded BIMCO, the world's largest shipping association with 2,200 members, to include SCMA BIMCO arbitration clause options in its standard contract templates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In 2013, SCMA has even managed to persuade the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO) to have SCMA BIMCO arbitration clause options in its many standard contract templates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: BIMCO is the world's largest shipping association with 2,200 members worldwide.

sections.label: Only London and New York
sections.summary: Before that, only London and New York made it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Before that, only London and New York made it.

sections.label: SICC and EU Hague Convention
sections.summary: The speaker says SICC should tap this, with EU states under the Hague Convention as key targets, since reciprocity currently extends only to Brunei and Malaysia.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We can and should tap on this for SICC, too.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Certainly, with the 27 states in the EU being contracting states under the Hague Convention, European parties must, certainly, be a key object of our persuasion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Currently, such reciprocity only extends to Brunei and Malaysia.

sections.label: Bill gives judgments enforceability
sections.summary: The Bill gives Court judgments an effect possibly similar to international arbitral awards for enforceability, with chosen courts in contracting states taking up disputes subject to exceptions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: What this Bill does is that it gives Court judgments an effect that might be similar to international arbitral awards as far as enforceability goes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The first, and this is reflected in Article 5 of the Convention as well as section 11 of the Bill, is that a court that is chosen, as long as it is one of the courts that is in the contracting states, these courts will have to take up the dispute, subject to certain exceptions.

sections.label: Courts must stay proceedings
sections.summary: Under Article 6 of the Convention and section 12 of the Bill, courts of party countries must stay or dismiss proceedings subject to another court's jurisdiction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The second is that – this is in Article 6 of the Convention as well as section 12 of the Bill – the courts of the countries that are parties to it must actually stay proceedings or dismiss proceedings if they are subject to the jurisdiction of another court.

sections.label: Enforcement of judgments
sections.summary: The final component is the enforcement of judgments, under Article 8 of the Convention and section 13 of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The final component is the enforcement of judgments and it is under Article 8 of the Convention and section 13 of the Bill.

sections.label: Bill parties and Convention signatories
sections.summary: The Bill applies only to Mexico, Singapore and most of the EU, and lacks the reach of an arbitral award due to Convention signatories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In fact, right now, the only parties to which this Bill will apply would be Mexico, Singapore and most of the EU, with one exception.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I believe that this Bill has tremendous potential but it still does not have the same reach as an arbitral award because of the number of signatories to the underlining Convention.

sections.label: Public policy carve-out and choice of law
sections.summary: Apart from one public policy carve-out, the answer is yes, making parties' clear choice of law important.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Well, the short answer is that apart from one carve-out for public policy, the answer would be yes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This is why it is quite important for parties to make a clear choice on the choice of law because, ultimately, it is for parties to choose which forum they like.

sections.label: Recognition of parties' chosen jurisdiction
sections.summary: International arbitral awards remain in force because parties' choice is recognised, and contracting states are recognised subject to public policy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But international arbitral awards are still in force, and that is because we recognise the choice of parties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: So, likewise over here, if parties choose a certain jurisdiction that happens to be a contracting state, then we are obliged to recognise that, subject to public policy and other considerations.

sections.label: Grounds to refuse foreign judgment enforcement
sections.summary: Courts must refuse recognition or enforcement of foreign judgments obtained by fraud, without notification, or incompatible with Singapore public policy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Courts must refuse to recognise or enforce a judgment where the foreign judgment was obtained by fraud in connection with the matter of procedure or when the defendant was not notified of the proceedings against it, and recognition or enforcement is incompatible with the public policy of Singapore.

sections.label: Clause 9(1)(b) excludes employment contracts
sections.summary: A clarification notes that clause 9(1)(b) of the Bill explicitly excludes employment contracts and collective agreements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Just one point of clarification for the Senior Minister of State.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: I noticed that clause 9(1)(b) of the Bill specifically or explicitly excludes employment contracts and collective agreements.

sections.label: Employment contracts excluded from Convention
sections.summary: The Bill excludes employment contracts because they are not covered in the Convention, which deals with international civil and commercial matters.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The reason why the Bill does not include things like employment contracts is because they are not covered in the Convention.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The reason for that is because this is a Convention that deals with international civil and commercial matters.
